title: Morphology of Flowering Plants
tagline: Root, stem, leaf, flower and fruit: the external plan of the flowering plant and its modifications.

overview.intro: Morphology is the study of external form, and it is the part of the course in which a drawing and a label list earn direct marks. This chapter works through the root and its modifications, the stem and the leaf with the forms and venation that distinguish monocot from dicot, the inflorescences, and the flower itself with the parts, symmetry and floral formula that let you read a specimen — then the fruit and seed, and the economic importance of each part. The examiner’s standing requests are to identify a specimen from its description, to draw and label a T.S. or a floral diagram, and to name the modification a structure represents and the function it performs.

facts.label: Root system
facts.value: Taproot in dicots with a primary root and laterals; fibrous root in monocots arising from the base of the stem.

facts.label: Leaf parts
facts.value: Lamina, leaf base, petiole and stipules, with reticulate venation in dicots and parallel venation in monocots.

facts.label: Floral whorls
facts.value: Calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium, described by a floral formula and drawn as a floral diagram.

facts.label: Inflorescence
facts.value: Racemose with an growing axis and indeterminate growth, and cymose with a terminal flower and determinate growth.

learningOutcomes: Describe the root and its modifications with the functions each performs.
Distinguish stem and root modifications, including underground and aerial forms.
Compare monocot and dicot leaves on venation, shape and parts.
Describe racemose and cymose inflorescences and the parts of a flower.
Read a floral formula and floral diagram and relate them to a specimen.

learn.title: Roots and stems, and their modifications

blocks.text: The root is the part of the plant that usually grows downward into the soil and has no nodes, no leaves and no internodes. A dicot seed produces a single primary root that grows deep and gives lateral branches, forming the taproot system of a mustard or a pea, and this system can persist as a taproot or be replaced by adventitious roots arising from any part of the stem or leaf. A monocot seed produces only a short-lived primary root replaced quickly by a mass of slender roots from the base of the stem, the fibrous root system of grass and wheat, which anchors the plant firmly but does not penetrate deeply. Root modifications serve functions the ordinary root cannot. In a turnip or a carrot the taproot swells into a fleshy store of food and water — a napiform or conical storage root — and it is this swollen part that we eat. Prop roots descend from the branches of a banyan and reach the soil, branching and thickening until they look like additional trunks and support the spreading crown. Stilt roots arise in rings from the lower nodes of a stem, as in maize and sugarcane, steadying the tall slender stem against wind. Haustorial roots in Cuscuta, a parasite, penetrate the tissues of the host plant and absorb ready-made food. pneumatophores, such as those of the mangrove Avicennia, grow upward out of waterlogged, oxygen-poor mud so that their tips can take in air through lenticels — the root breathing against the direction of gravity. The stem, by contrast, bears nodes and internodes, buds in the axils of leaves, and grows upward toward light. Its modifications are equally varied. Underground stems store food and let the plant survive a harsh season: the potato is a modified stem bearing eyes, which are axillary buds, and its nodes and scale leaves are still visible; the ginger rhizome shows the same features with buds on its surface; onion and garlic are layers of fleshy leaf bases on a very short stem; and in the onion the flat ring-like structure is the leaf bases while the disc at the base is the stem proper. Aerial modifications include tendrils in the passionflower and grape, which are shoots that coil around supports, and phylloclades in Opuntia and Casuarina, where the stem has become flattened and green and carries out photosynthesis in place of the leaves. Thorns in Bougainvillea and Citrus are modified axillary buds, which is what distinguishes a thorn from a prickle.

items: The root has no nodes, no internodes and no leaves and grows downward.
Taproot in dicots: a persistent primary root with laterals; fibrous root in monocots from the stem base.
Storage roots: napiform turnip, conical carrot, fasciculated asparagus.
Prop roots of the banyan and stilt roots of maize support the plant; haustoria absorb from a host.
Pneumatophores grow upward in mangrove mud to take in air through lenticels.
The stem bears nodes, internodes, axillary buds and grows towards light.
Underground stems — potato, ginger, rhizome, corm — store food and carry buds.
A potato eye is an axillary bud, which is what marks it as a stem rather than a root.
Tendrils are modified shoots; phylloclades are flattened photosynthetic stems; thorns are buds.

items.note: Each eye is an axillary bud with its own meristem, so a piece of potato with an eye grows a whole new plant — a root piece could not do this.
In a swamp the mud blocks oxygen, so the mangrove root grows against gravity to reach the air.

blocks.text: A leaf normally arises from a node and consists of a flat lamina, a leaf base attaching it to the stem, a stalk or petiole holding it out into the light, and in many plants a pair of stipules at the base of the petiole. The lamina has a midrib with veins branching from them, and the pattern of those veins separates the two great groups: dicots show reticulate, net-like venation as in a mango or hibiscus leaf, while monocots show parallel venation as in grass, maize and lily, with the veins running the length of the blade. Leaf shape, margin, apex and surface are all used in identification — a leaf may be ovate, lanceolate, linear or heart-shaped, with an entire, serrate or lobed margin. Simple leaves have an undivided lamina; compound leaves, such as the neem or the rose, have the lamina divided into leaflets, and the division is pinnate, as in neem, or palmate, as in China rose. Venation and leaf type are matched to habitat: the narrow leaves of a xerophyte reduce water loss, the large drip tips of rainforest leaves shed excess water, and needle leaves with a thick cuticle, as in pine, are an adaptation to dryness as much as to cold. Some leaves are modified for special work — the tendrils of peas are leaflets, the spines of cactus reduce transpiration, the pitcher of Nepenthes traps insects, and the fleshy leaves of aloe store water. Leaves may also be arranged on the stem in three patterns: alternate, with one leaf at each node as in mustard; opposite, with two at each node as in guava and Calotropis; and whorled, with three or more at a node as in Alstonia. The arrangement ensures that leaves do not shade one another, which is the point of the pattern rather than the pattern itself. Inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers on the axis, and it is of two basic kinds. Racemose has an axis that continues to grow at the tip, so new flowers are added at the apex while the older, larger ones are at the base — an indeterminate growth pattern — and its forms include the simple raceme of mustard, the spike of Veronica, the umbel of onion, the corymb of candytuft and the capitulum or head of sunflower, in which many small flowers sit on a flat receptacle. Cymose has the axis ending in a flower, so growth stops there and further flowers arise from lateral branches below it — a determinate pattern — giving the uniparous cyme of jasmine, the biparous cyme of Datura and the multiparous cyme of Calotropis.

items: A leaf has lamina, leaf base, petiole and often stipules, and arises at a node.
Reticulate venation marks dicots; parallel venation marks monocots.
Simple leaves have an undivided lamina; compound leaves are pinnate or palmate.
Leaf arrangement is alternate, opposite or whorled, arranged to avoid shading.
Modified leaves: tendrils in pea, spines in cactus, pitchers in Nepenthes, storage in aloe.
Drip tips and needle leaves are habitat adaptations of the lamina.
Racemose inflorescence grows indeterminately with the oldest flowers lowest.
Forms of racemose: raceme, spike, umbel, corymb and capitulum.
Cymose inflorescence ends in a flower so growth is determinate.
Cymose forms: uniparous in jasmine, biparous in Datura, multiparous in Calotropis.

items.note: What looks like one flower is a capitulum of many small florets on a common receptacle — count the ray florets to see it.
The alternate arrangement sets each leaf at an angle to the one below so that few are fully shaded.

learn.title: The flower, the floral formula and economic products

blocks.text: The flower is the reproductive shoot, borne on a stalk called the pedicel with a swollen receptacle at its tip from which the four whorls arise: the calyx of sepals, the corolla of petals, the androecium of stamens and the gynoecium of carpels. A flower is complete when it has all four whorls and incomplete when one is missing; it is bisexual when it carries both androecium and gynoecium and unisexual when it carries only one, in which case it is staminate or pistillate. Symmetry is of two kinds: an actinomorphic flower can be divided into equal halves by any plane through the centre, as a mustard or chilli flower can, while a zygomorphic flower can be divided in only one plane, as a pea or a bean can — a shape that guides a pollinating insect to one particular position. The parts are described by a floral formula, a shorthand that gives the number and fusion of each whorl: K for calyx, C for corolla, A for androecium, G for gynoecium, with a bar over the G meaning superior and a bar below meaning inferior, a plus sign inside a circle meaning polyandrous, and numbers joined by a bracket meaning fusion — so K(5) means five fused sepals and C1+1+(2)+(2) describes the irregular pea corolla of one standard, two wings and two fused keel petals. The corresponding floral diagram is a drawing of the flower as seen from above, showing each whorl as concentric symbols with the mother axis marked behind — together the formula and the diagram identify a specimen without any ambiguity. Fruits and seeds complete the story and carry the economic importance. A fruit develops from the ovary and may be fleshy, as the mango with its exocarp, mesocarp and endocarp, or dry, as the groundnut and the capsule. The seed holds the embryo and its food, and its products feed the world: wheat and rice give starch, pulses give protein, oil seeds such as groundnut and mustard give oil, and sugar comes from sugarcane and beet. Beyond food, the plant body supplies cotton fibre from the seed coat, jute and flax from stem fibre, timber from wood, rubber from the latex of Hevea, and drugs and spices from leaves, bark and seeds — which is why morphology is not merely an academic exercise but the basis of agriculture and industry.

items: The four whorls arise from the receptacle: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium.
Complete or incomplete by whorls present; bisexual or unisexual by sex organs present.
Actinomorphic flowers divide in any plane; zygomorphic flowers in one plane only.
The floral formula records K, C, A and G with fusion and the position of the ovary.
A bar above G means superior ovary, below means inferior.
The floral diagram shows the whorls from above with the mother axis marked.
Fruits are fleshy or dry and develop from the ovary wall after fertilisation.
Seeds supply starch, protein and oil; stems supply fibre and timber.
Latex, drugs and spices come from various parts and complete the economic account.

blocks.text: Morphology is examined as much by description as by recall, and a description earns marks when it follows a fixed order and uses the technical vocabulary precisely. For a vegetative specimen, begin with the root: is there one main root or many arising from the stem base, which separates a taproot plant from a fibrous one? Then the stem — is it above ground, underground or modified, and does it bear nodes, scale leaves or eyes that mark it as a stem? Then the leaves: their arrangement on the stem, whether the lamina is simple or compound, its shape, its margin, and above all its venation, since reticulate veins indicate a dicot and parallel veins a monocot. For a floral specimen, work through the whorls in order and count the parts of each, noting whether the parts are free or fused — a fused calyx is written as one unit in a formula while a free one counts separately — then observe the symmetry by attempting to divide the flower in more than one plane, and finally look below the flower at the ovary to judge whether it sits above or below the attachment of the other whorls, which gives the superior or inferior position. The habit that converts a description into marks is to state the function alongside the feature whenever the question allows: veins are not merely reticulate, they are reticulate and branching so that every part of the lamula is supplied and supported; a swollen base is not merely swollen, it stores food for the next season. Two common errors are worth avoiding. Do not name a structure without the character that identifies it — saying the plant has a taproot is worth less than saying it has a single main root with laterals arising from it. And do not confuse organs that look alike in function: a tendril of the pea is a modified leaflet while a tendril of the passionflower is a modified shoot, and only the position tells you which. Practising on specimens in this order — root, stem, leaf, inflorescence, flower, fruit — is exactly how the practical paper is marked.

items: Describe in order: root, stem, leaf, inflorescence, flower, fruit.
Root first: single main root with laterals gives taproot; many from the stem base gives fibrous.
Stem features are nodes, internodes, scale leaves and buds — no root carries them.
Leaf description covers arrangement, whether simple or compound, shape, margin and venation.
Reticulate venation indicates a dicot; parallel venation indicates a monocot.
Flower description counts and states fusion of each whorl, then symmetry, then ovary position.
State the function with the feature wherever the question allows it.
Never name a structure without the character that identifies it.

keyPoints: The root lacks nodes, internodes and leaves; the stem has all three and bears axillary buds.
Dicots have a taproot and reticulate venation; monocots have a fibrous root and parallel venation.
Storage roots include turnip and carrot; storage stems include potato, ginger and onion.
Prop roots, stilt roots, haustoria and pneumatophores serve support, parasitism and breathing.
Tendrils and phylloclades are stem modifications; tendrils of the pea are leaf modifications.
Leaves are alternate, opposite or whorled, an arrangement that avoids mutual shading.
Racemose inflorescence grows indeterminately; cymose ends in a flower.
The flower has four whorls arising from the receptacle.
Actinomorphic flowers divide in any plane; zygomorphic flowers in one only.
The floral formula and floral diagram describe a flower unambiguously.
Fruits develop from the ovary and may be fleshy or dry.
Plant products supply food, fibre, timber, rubber, drugs and spices.
examFocus: Identification answers name the modification and then the function it performs.
Leaf questions compare dicot and monocot on venation, shape and stipules together.
Inflorescence answers state which axis grows and where the oldest flower lies.
Floral formula questions want each symbol decoded, including ovary position.
Drawings must be labelled with the parts named in full, not lettered alone.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a modification of a stem?
questions.explanation: The potato tuber bears eyes, which are axillary buds, and nodes with scale leaves — the marks of a stem.
Monocot leaves such as grass and maize have veins running the length of the blade.

questions.prompt: In a cymose inflorescence the main axis:
questions.explanation: The axis terminates in a flower, so further flowers arise from below — determinate growth.
They grow upward out of oxygen-poor mud so their tips can take in air through lenticels.

questions.prompt: A flower that can be divided into equal halves by any plane through the centre is called __________.
questions.explanation: A zygomorphic flower, by contrast, divides in only one plane.

questions.prompt: In a floral formula, a bar written below the letter G indicates a __________ ovary.
questions.explanation: A bar above G indicates the opposite, an inferior ovary below the other whorls.

questions.prompt: Give three functions of root modifications other than absorption and anchorage.
questions.answer: Prop roots, such as those of the banyan, descend from the branches and, on reaching the soil, thicken into woody pillars that support the heavy spreading crown of the tree. Stilt roots arise in rings from the lower nodes of grasses such as maize and sugarcane and brace the tall slender stem against wind and flooding, anchoring it more firmly than the fibrous roots alone. Pneumatophores, as in the mangrove Avicennia, grow upward from the roots in waterlogged, oxygen-poor mud so that their tips, which bear lenticels, can take in the atmospheric oxygen the buried roots cannot obtain.
questions.explanation: Three modifications with the structure and the function each performs.

questions.prompt: How would you distinguish a simple leaf from a compound one, and give an example of each?
questions.answer: A simple leaf has an undivided lamina: the blade may be lobed or have a toothed margin, but the incisions never reach the midrib, so there is one blade arising from the leaf base. A compound leaf has the lamina divided entirely into separate leaflets, each arising from a common axis called the rachis, and the axillary bud at its base confirms that the whole structure is one leaf rather than a shoot bearing several. Compound leaves are of two kinds: pinnate, where the leaflets are arranged along both sides of the rachis as in the neem or rose, and palmate, where the leaflets radiate from a single point at the tip of the petiole as in the China rose and silk cotton. Examples: a mango leaf is simple, a neem leaf is pinnately compound.
questions.explanation: The criterion of the incision reaching the midrib, the bud test, the two kinds of compound, and an example of each.

questions.prompt: State two differences between a racemose and a cymose inflorescence.
questions.answer: In a racemose inflorescence the main axis continues to grow, so growth is indeterminate; new flowers are produced at the tip while the older and larger flowers lie at the base. In a cymose inflorescence the main axis ends in a flower and growth stops there, so further flowers arise from lateral branches below it and the oldest flower is at the tip. Their forms differ accordingly: racemose takes the shape of a raceme, spike, umbel, corymb or capitulum, while cymose is uniparous, biparous or multiparous.
questions.explanation: Growth of the axis and the position of the oldest flower, with the forms of each.

questions.prompt: Describe the underground modifications of the stem with an example of each, and explain how you would tell them from modified roots.
questions.answer: Underground stems are modified for storage and for perennation, and they retain the diagnostic features of a stem even when buried. The rhizome is a horizontally growing underground stem, as in ginger and turmeric, which is flattened, bears nodes and internodes with scale leaves at the nodes, and produces axillary buds that grow upward into new shoots — the knobbly appearance of ginger is exactly these bud and scale features. The tuber is an enlarged terminal or lateral bud swollen with stored food, and the potato shows the type clearly: its eyes are axillary buds arranged spirally around the tuber, each with a scale leaf beneath it, and each eye can sprout into a shoot. The corm is a short, thick, vertical stem that stores food for one season, as in Colocasia and Amorphophallus, with a definite terminal bud at the top and nodes bearing scale leaves around the body. In the onion and garlic the store is different again: the layers are fleshy leaf bases arising from an extremely short stem, the flat disc at the base being the stem proper, so the food is in the leaves rather than the stem. The way to tell a modified stem from a modified root is to look for the stem characters: nodes, internodes, scale leaves and axillary buds or eyes. A turnip or carrot has none of these — no nodes, no buds, no scale leaves — and instead shows the remains of root hairs and the branching of laterals, which identifies it as a root. Buds are the decisive test, since roots never bear them.
questions.explanation: Each modification with example and its stem features, then the explicit distinguishing criteria.

questions.prompt: A plant is described as having a stout horizontal underground structure with distinct nodes, scale leaves at each node and buds on the upper surface, from which leafy shoots arise. Identify the structure and explain why it is not a root, giving two other examples of the same modification and the function all of them share.
questions.answer: The structure is a rhizome, a horizontally growing modification of the stem. Its identity rests on the three characters that define a stem wherever it is found: distinct nodes and internodes, scale leaves borne at the nodes, and buds arising from the axils of those leaves, from which the leafy shoots are growing upward. The buds on the upper surface are axillary or terminal buds with their own meristems, each capable of developing into a shoot — which is what allows the plant to spread laterally and to regenerate after the aerial parts die back. It is not a root because a root has none of these features: a root grows downward, bears no nodes or internodes, has no true leaves or leaf scales, and never carries buds, so no root can produce a shoot directly from its surface. Two further examples of the same modification are ginger and turmeric, both of which show the same flattened form with nodes, scale leaves and buds, and the potato tuber, which is an enlarged underground stem bud bearing eyes with scale leaves beneath them. The function these share is storage: the stem becomes swollen with starch and other reserves so that the plant can survive an unfavourable season underground and sprout again when conditions return, combining a food store with a means of vegetative propagation.
questions.explanation: Identification with the stem characters, the explicit contrast with roots, two examples, and the shared function of storage and perennation.

questions.prompt: Explain how leaf modifications adapt a plant to its habitat, giving three examples.
questions.answer: Leaves are the organs most exposed to the environment, so where conditions are harsh they are the first to be modified, and each modification answers a specific environmental problem. In a cactus, leaves are reduced to sharp spines, which does far more than defence: a spine has a very small surface area relative to its volume and often a thick cuticle, so the water lost by transpiration is drastically reduced, while the photosynthetic work is transferred to the flattened green stem — the adaptation of a plant to a desert where water loss would otherwise be fatal. In Nepenthes, the pitcher plant of nutrient-poor soils, the leaf is modified into a hollow pitcher with a lid and digestive glands inside; insects are attracted, fall in and are digested, supplying nitrogen and minerals that the soil lacks, which allows the plant to colonise habitats where other plants starve. In the pea, the terminal leaflets are drawn out into coiling tendrils that grasp any support they touch, letting a weak-stemmed plant climb towards light in crowded vegetation rather than being shaded out. A fourth example worth knowing is the fleshy water-storing leaf of aloe and Bryophyllum, whose thick parenchyma holds reserves against drought — and Bryophlyllum further carries adventitious buds in the notches of its leaf margin, so a fallen leaf can grow a whole plant. Across all of them the principle is the same: the lamina is altered to reduce water loss, capture scarce nutrients, reach light or store water, and the plant survives where an ordinary leaf would fail.
questions.explanation: Three or more modifications, each with the environmental problem and the structural answer.
